before: map[string]int maps String keys to int values. A map literal creates initialized map storage.
Assigning a map variable does not clone its entries. Mutating through an alias is visible through the original.
A map’s nil zero value supports reading and len, but assignment of an entry requires an initialized map, such as one made with make or a literal.
Do not depend on map iteration order for deterministic output. This example looks up a known key directly.

Optional local transfer task: Compare a map alias with explicitly copying entries into a newly initialized map. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A map matches keys to values. A key is the label used to find an entry. `map[string]int` uses text keys and whole-number values.
`alias := counts` gives another way to reach the same map. It does not copy the entries into a new map.
A map starts at nil if no storage is supplied. You can read it and check its length, but writing an entry needs an initialized map. `make` or a map value written with braces provides that storage.
Go does not promise an order when visiting map entries. Here, a direct lookup finds the known key read.
The screen shows `5`. Both names reach the same map entry.
Change the assignment through alias from 5 to 7. The lookup through counts still reads that shared entry.
